sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: first-arrival versus same-time yielding, steady versus flashing lights, railroad signs and work zone controls
Confusable pairs among the yielding rules, steady and flashing signals, warning and railroad signs and work zone controls, followed by continuation facts; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec07-R01 | anchor: A02
The Same Time Rule only applies when both drivers reach a stop-sign-controlled four-way intersection together, and then the driver on the left gives way to the driver on the right. [A02]
Why it matters: group right-of-way; confusable arriving first versus arriving together.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec07-R02 | anchor: A02
Turning left, you give way to oncoming drivers; entering from a ramp, a driveway or a private road, you give way to drivers already on the road you are joining. [A02]
Why it matters: group right-of-way; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec07-R03 | anchor: A02
Some intersections and other locations have signals with lights of only one color, either green, yellow or red. [A02]
Why it matters: group signals; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec07-R04 | anchor: A03
A steady yellow tells you to stop and wait for the next green, while a flashing yellow lets you keep going slowly with caution, ready to stop for entering traffic. [A03]
Why it matters: group signals; confusable steady yellow versus flashing yellow.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec07-R05 | anchor: A03
As you approach a yellow light, watch for and allow for mistakes by other drivers beside, ahead of and behind you. [A03]
Why it matters: group signals; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec07-R06 | anchor: A04
After a complete stop at a flashing red you may enter once you have looked both ways and yielded where needed, which is the stop sign procedure rather than a wait for green. [A04]
Why it matters: group signals; confusable flashing red versus steady red.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec07-R07 | anchor: A04
The manual highlights only a selection of signs of interest to drivers and says it does not cover every sign. [A04]
Why it matters: group signs; difficulty low.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec07-R08 | anchor: A06
The round yellow RR sign gives advance warning before the crossing, while the white X-shaped Railroad Crossing sign marks the crossing itself. [A06]
Why it matters: group railroad; confusable advance warning sign versus crossing sign.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec07-R09 | anchor: A06
Not every crossing with more than one track has a track-count sign, so check for extra tracks, trains or railroad vehicles at every crossing. [A06]
Why it matters: group railroad; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec07-R10 | anchor: A07
Once you start across railroad tracks you keep going without stopping, but a stop required by traffic or a signal is made at the stop line before you reach the tracks. [A07]
Why it matters: group railroad; confusable crossing without stopping versus stopping before the tracks.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec07-R11 | anchor: A07
Work zone signs are orange and may be diamond or rectangular, and they cover construction, maintenance and emergency operations. [A07]
Why it matters: group work zones; confusable orange work zone sign versus yellow warning sign.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec07-R12 | anchor: A08
Besides guiding traffic, work zone barriers can block drivers from closed roads and from other places where driving would be dangerous. [A08]
Why it matters: group work zones; difficulty low.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0066]
